862.title: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)
862.hook: a dying grandfather tells the new king that ruling well looks a lot like being pregnant
862.tomorrow: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)

segments.voice: Yesterday Shanti opened: Krishna stepped aside, God standing to one side, and Bhishma, cleared of pain, began to teach.

What is a king for? It sounds like a question for a political science class, but on the field it's urgent. Yudhishthira wears the crown now, and he still half wants to run. So he asks his grandfather plainly what a king's duties are. Bhishma's answer fills a long section of the Shanti Parva, known as Rajadharma, the dharma of kings. It's practical, sometimes blunt, full of advice about treasuries, spies and alliances. But a few pictures in it stick: a pond full of fish, and a mother carrying a child.
screen: `WHAT IS A KING FOR?` → `RAJADHARMA.` → `FISH, AND A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: First, the fish. Bhishma describes what happens when no one keeps order. The strong devour the weak, he says, the way big fish eat the little ones in the water. Nobody's property is safe, nobody's family is safe, and the strong do whatever they like. The point isn't that kings are grand. It's that the weak need someone standing between them and the strong. In Bhishma's teaching, that's the job: protection before glory. Second, the mother. A king, Bhishma says, should act like an expectant mother. A woman carrying a child, in his picture, sets aside some of what she'd like for herself, for the good of the child. So a king sets aside his own likes for the good of his people. It's a striking image from a warrior who vowed never to marry or have children. The ruler, in his teaching, isn't the one being served. He's the one carrying. Underneath runs a warning. Again and again Bhishma tells Yudhishthira to be gentle without being weak, and firm without being cruel. A king who is always soft gets ignored; one who is always harsh gets feared and hated. And Yudhishthira, who wanted to run to the forest, is being told that ruling well is itself a kind of self-denial. Peace, for him, may not mean escaping the throne. It may mean carrying it.
screen: `BIG FISH EAT THE SMALL` · `PROTECTION BEFORE GLORY` · `A KING LIKE AN EXPECTANT MOTHER` · then, large: `GENTLE, BUT NOT WEAK`

segments.voice: Rest one hand lightly over your belly and bring to mind the people who depend on you, at home, at work, anywhere, and one thing you already set aside for their sake. Then think of one person who is the small fish somewhere in your world, and simply hold them in mind; if you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.
Rajadharma. The dharma of kings: protect the small fish, and carry your people the way a mother carries a child.
Your line: carry them like a mother. Tomorrow, what to do when the rules run out. Day eight hundred sixty-two, done.

863.title: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)
863.hook: in a famine, a great sage creeps into a hut at night to steal a piece of dog meat, and gets caught
863.carry: a dead sage helps no one
863.tomorrow: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)
863.howItsDone: Hindu teachers and writers on dharma discuss Apaddharma, the conduct allowed in real distress, and the story of Vishvamitra and the dog meat is told as a hard example of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday Bhishma said a king stands between the big fish and the small, and carries his people like a mother. Your line was carry them like a mother.

Yudhishthira asks a hard question. What happens to dharma when everything falls apart? When there's war, famine, collapse, and the normal rules can't be kept? Bhishma's answer is a whole section called Apaddharma, dharma in times of distress. To explain it, he tells a story that's uncomfortable on purpose. A great sage, Vishvamitra, is starving. The rains have failed for a long time. The fields are dust, the villages empty, and people eat whatever they can find. One night, half dead, Vishvamitra slips into a poor hamlet looking for food.
screen: `WHEN THE RULES RUN OUT.` → `APADDHARMA.` → `A STARVING SAGE AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: In one hut he sees the haunch of a dog hanging. For a man of his station, by the rules of his world, this is deeply forbidden food. He decides to steal it anyway. But the man who lives there wakes and catches him, and what follows isn't a fight. It's a debate. The householder, a man the society of that time placed at the bottom, argues for the rules. You're a sage, he says. You know dharma. Don't do this. Even I wouldn't advise it. Vishvamitra argues back. Staying alive comes first, because only the living can practice dharma at all. When I'm through this, I'll make amends with austerity. A dead sage helps no one. The householder isn't fully convinced, but Vishvamitra takes the meat, and even now, the story says, he means to offer it to the gods before he eats. Then the god Indra sends rain, and the plants and the people revive. The story leaves the discomfort in place. The great sage steals. The man at the bottom lectures him on dharma. And Bhishma's point to the new king is that dharma in a disaster isn't the same as dharma on an ordinary day. Rules exist to protect life. When keeping them would end life, a wise person may have to bend them, and then repair what they broke. But this is for real distress, Bhishma warns, not convenience. A king who calls every inconvenience a famine, in effect, has missed the lesson.
screen: `THE FORBIDDEN FOOD` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER ARGUES FOR THE RULES` · `"ONLY THE LIVING PRACTICE DHARMA"` · then, large: `FOR REAL DISTRESS ONLY`

segments.voice: Let your breath settle and bring to mind a time you bent one of your own rules because things were falling apart. Breathe in and remember what was at stake; breathe out and ask honestly, without judging yourself, whether it was a real emergency or just convenience, and whether anything still needs repairing. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer.
Apaddharma. Dharma for times of distress: a starving sage who stole forbidden food, and the man who argued with him.
Your line: a dead sage helps no one. Tomorrow, a pair of pigeons and a hunter. See you then.

segments.voice: A storm breaks over the forest. A hunter, a hard man who lives by trapping birds, is caught out in it, soaked and shaking with cold. In his cage is a female pigeon he caught that day. He crouches under a big tree for shelter, not knowing the tree is her home. Up in its branches her mate is grieving, wondering where she's gone. And from inside the cage, she can hear him. Yudhishthira had asked about a person who gives shelter to someone who asks for it. This is the story Bhishma tells.
screen: `A STORM IN THE FOREST.` → `A HUNTER UNDER THEIR TREE.` → `SHE HEARS HER MATE.`

segments.voice: The female pigeon calls up to her mate, and what she says is startling. Don't grieve for me. This man has come to our home, cold and hungry. He's our guest. Treat him as one. And the male pigeon does. He fetches a burning ember from somewhere, gathers dry leaves, and makes a fire so the hunter can warm himself. Then he realizes he has nothing to feed his guest, no store of grain, nothing set aside. So he offers himself, and drops into the fire, so the hunter will have food. The hunter is undone. The man who caught birds for a living has just watched a bird give its life to feed him. He opens the cage and lets the female go. But she, grieving her mate, follows him into the fire too, and the story says the two rise to heaven together, shining. The hunter can't go back to who he was. He throws away his nets and his cage, gives up hunting, and goes into the forest to live in austerity. The word underneath all this is atithi, the guest. In the dharma Bhishma teaches, a guest at your door is to be honored, whoever they are, even an enemy, even the person who hurt you. It's an extreme story, and the text tells it as extreme. Bhishma isn't asking the new king to leap into fires. He's showing how far hospitality reaches: past fairness, past safety, all the way to the person who did you harm.
screen: `"HE IS OUR GUEST"` · `A FIRE FOR THE HUNTER` · `THE PIGEON GIVES HIMSELF` · then, large: `THE HUNTER LAYS DOWN HIS NETS`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open and bring to mind someone who will come through your door, or your inbox, or your day, who isn't easy to welcome. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer.
atithi. Guest: the one who comes to your door, to be honored, whoever they are, even the person who hurt you.

865.title: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)
865.hook: a hunter drags a snake to a grieving mother so she can watch it die, and she tells him to let it go
865.tomorrow: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)
865.howItsDone: The story of Gautami, the snake, Death and Time is retold by Hindu teachers when they speak of karma and of letting go of revenge, and it stands at the opening of the Anushasana Parva.

segments.voice: Yesterday a pigeon honored the hunter who trapped his mate. Your line was the hunter laid down his nets.

After all of Bhishma's teaching, Yudhishthira is still stuck in the same place. I caused all this, he says. I'm the reason you're lying on those arrows. So when the Anushasana Parva opens, Bhishma answers with a story about blame. An old woman named Gautami finds her son dead. A snake has bitten him. A hunter, Arjunaka, catches the snake, ties it with a cord, and drags it to her. Tell me how to kill it, he says. Fire, or cut it to pieces? Either is fine with me.
screen: `"I CAUSED ALL THIS."` → `A BOY BITTEN BY A SNAKE.` → `"HOW SHALL I KILL IT?"`

segments.voice: Gautami says: let it go. Killing it won't bring my son back, and it won't make me any less sad. The hunter argues; surely the guilty should pay. Then the snake speaks up. Don't blame me. I didn't act on my own. Death sent me. And Death, Mrityu, appears. Don't blame me either. I was directed by Time. Then Time itself, Kala, arrives and says: none of us is the real cause. The boy's own past actions, his karma, brought him here. We were only the instruments. Gautami listens and accepts it. The hunter lets the snake go. Death and Time depart. It's a strange chain, and Bhishma means it to be. Each link points at the next, and the chain ends not in a villain but in the long working of actions and their results. Now look at who's listening. Yudhishthira is sure he's the snake, that the deaths are on him alone. Bhishma is saying, gently, that you are one link in something much longer, and you are not the whole of it. This isn't permission to stop caring. It's a way out of the kind of guilt that eats a person alive and helps nobody. And notice who sees it first. Not the warrior, not the king. A grieving old mother, with every reason to want revenge, is the one who says let it go. Anushasana means instruction, and its opening lesson, in this story, is about where blame stops.
screen: `"LET IT GO"` · `THE SNAKE, DEATH, AND TIME` · `THE CHAIN ENDS IN KARMA` · then, large: `YOU ARE NOT THE WHOLE OF IT`

segments.voice: Soften your jaw and bring to mind something you still blame yourself for, and look honestly at your part in it. Then, breath by breath, let the other causes come into view, other people, timing, things nobody chose; you don't have to excuse anything, just let the picture be its true size. If you pray, you can bring that weight into your prayer.
Anushasana. Instruction: the book that opens with Gautami's story of the snake, Death and Time, and a mother who says let it go.

866.title: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Gautami's story, the chain of blame ran back through the snake, Death and Time. Your line was let it go.

Bhishma carries an unusual gift. Long ago, his father blessed him so that death would come only when he chose it. So he has been lying on the arrows, teaching, and waiting for a particular turning of the year: the time when the sun begins its northward course, called uttarayana, which the tradition holds as an auspicious time to die. He sent Yudhishthira back to the city to rule. Now the season has turned, and Yudhishthira returns to the field with fire, garlands and everything needed for the last rites.
screen: `DEATH ONLY WHEN HE CHOOSES.` → `WAITING FOR THE SUN TO TURN.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA RETURNS.`

segments.voice: Bhishma opens his eyes and sees them all around him: Yudhishthira and his brothers, Dhritarashtra, Gandhari, Kunti, Krishna. The time has come, he says. He tells Dhritarashtra, the blind king whose sons are gone, not to grieve, and to treat the Pandavas as his own. Then he turns to Krishna and asks for leave to go. A man who can choose his own death still asks permission to take it. Krishna gives it. And then Bhishma does something the text describes almost like a meditation. He draws his life breath inward, part by part. As it withdraws from each limb, the story says, the arrows in that part fall away and the wound closes. Limb by limb, the bed of arrows lets him go. At last the breath leaves through the crown of his head, rising like a great light into the sky. His family builds the pyre and performs the rites, then goes down to the Ganga to offer water. The river goddess herself rises from it, weeping. Bhishma was her son, and she grieves that he fell to Shikhandi. Krishna comforts her: it was Arjuna who brought him down, with Shikhandi only standing in front, and her son has gone to the heavens. Don't grieve. So the teaching from the bed of arrows ends without a speech: a man finishing his work, asking leave, and going when it's time, while the arrows fall from him one by one.

segments.voice: Let your body be heavy and supported, and with each slow out-breath let one part soften and let go: your feet, your legs, your belly, your shoulders, your face. Take your time, part by part, the way the arrows fell away; there's nothing to finish right now. If you pray, you can rest in your prayer as you let go.

The water offerings for Bhishma have been poured into the Ganga. The great teacher is gone. Yudhishthira has listened to him at length, about kingship, duty and peace. He has the crown and the kingdom. And at the riverbank, in Ganguli's telling, he simply goes down, collapsing on the bank, overwhelmed by grief. Bhima holds him. Krishna speaks to him. segments.voice: Ashvamedhika is the book of the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice: a great royal rite in which a consecrated horse wanders free, guarded by warriors, and the kingdoms it passes through either welcome it or fight. The idea isn't Yudhishthira's. He wants to leave the throne for the forest. It's the sage Vyasa who tells him that grief is not a plan. Perform sacrifices, Vyasa says, give gifts, take up a king's work; the horse sacrifice will cleanse what weighs on you. Yudhishthira's answer is practical. There's no money. The war has emptied the treasury, the kings who might have sent tribute are dead, and he will not squeeze grieving people for more. So Vyasa tells an old story. Long ago, King Marutta held a sacrifice in the Himalayas so lavish that the gold left behind was too much to carry away. It's still there in the mountains, Vyasa says. Go and bring it. The victors don't get a parade. They get a man who can't stand up, an empty treasury, and a sage pointing at an old king's leftover gold. The way forward runs through someone else's generosity, long ago. In the days ahead, this book brings a forgotten teaching, an angry sage, a child who comes back to life, a son who fights his father, and a strange little animal with half a golden body. It begins with getting up.
screen: `ASHVAMEDHA: THE HORSE SACRIFICE` · `VYASA: GRIEF IS NOT A PLAN` · `"THE TREASURY IS EMPTY"` · then, large: `MARUTTA'S GOLD IN THE MOUNTAINS`

Breathe out, let your shoulders drop, and hold the name of one person near you who may be on the riverbank right now; if you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.

868.title: Ashvamedhika
868.hook: after the war, in a quiet palace hall, Arjuna admits to Krishna that he has forgotten the teaching he heard on the battlefield
868.howItsDone: The Anugita is read by students of the Mahabharata alongside the Bhagavad Gita, and commentators and teachers in several Hindu traditions have discussed how the two teachings relate.

segments.voice: Yesterday Ashvamedhika opened with Yudhishthira on the riverbank, an empty treasury, and Vyasa pointing to old King Marutta's gold. Your line was a man who can't stand up.

I've forgotten it. That, in plain terms, is what Arjuna tells Krishna. The war is over. The two friends are walking in the great assembly hall the Pandavas have won back, with time on their hands at last. And Arjuna brings up the conversation in the chariot, between the two armies, before the fighting began: the teaching people now call the Bhagavad Gita. What you told me then, he says, has slipped from my mind. Please tell it to me again.
screen: `THE WAR IS OVER.` → `A WALK IN THE HALL.` → `"I'VE FORGOTTEN IT."`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't pretend that's fine. In Ganguli's telling he's displeased. You didn't hold on to what I told you in confidence, he says, and I'm sorry you forgot it. Then something surprising: he can't simply repeat it. He spoke on the battlefield, he explains, while united in yoga, and he can't call it back word for word. So instead he tells Arjuna an old story. A brahmana meets a perfected sage, a siddha, and asks the big questions: how a living being dies, how it is born again, what binds it to action, and how it goes free. The siddha answers at length. Then come more old dialogues: a brahmana and his wife, a teacher and his student. Together these chapters are known as the Anugita. They return to the Gita's ground, the self, action and freedom, but in a different shape: no army, no chariot, no crisis, just questions asked in peace. There's something honest in this. The first conversation happened between two armies, with war about to begin, and afterward even Arjuna, who heard it face to face, lost hold of it. Insight doesn't keep by itself. The teacher's answer isn't a recording. It's a new conversation, built for a calmer day. Krishna doesn't hand Arjuna the old words. He sits down in the hall and starts again.
screen: `KRISHNA IS DISPLEASED` · `"I SPOKE IT IN YOGA"` · `A SAGE ANSWERS A BRAHMANA` · then, large: `THE ANUGITA: THE TEACHING RETOLD`

segments.voice: Bring back one thing you once understood clearly, a lesson, a promise to yourself, something someone wise told you, that has faded since.
